title: Query Transformation Techniques
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Query Transformation Techniques ##### The question that could not be embedded A team in Hyderabad had a well-built RAG system over their engineering handbook — hybrid search, a reranker, contextual retrieval, everything from the last three days. It worked well. Then they analysed the queries it failed on, and a pattern emerged. The failures were almost all short: > "on-call?" > "how many days" > "what about contractors" Three to five words, no context, heavy reliance on what the user had asked previously or on knowledge they assumed. Embedding "on-call?" produces a vector near nothing in particular. BM25 matches the word "call" across two hundred documents about phone support. The average failed query was 4.1 words. The average successful one was 11.7. **The query is the weakest link in the retrieval pipeline**, and it is the one component you do not control. Users write badly, briefly, and with terminology that does not match your corpus. Query transformation is the layer that fixes this before retrieval happens — and it took the Hyderabad system from 76% to 91% on short queries. ##### The transformation toolkit ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Raw user query"] --> R{"Router"} R -->|"no retrieval needed"| D["Answer directly"] R -->|"ambiguous / short"| C["Contextualize
from conversation"] R -->|"vocabulary mismatch"| W["Rewrite"] R -->|"complex"| DE["Decompose"] R -->|"conceptual"| H["HyDE"] R -->|"broad"| M["Multi-query"] C --> RET["Retrieve"] W --> RET DE --> RET H --> RET M --> RET RET --> F["Fuse (RRF)"] F --> RR["Rerank"] RR --> G["Generate"] ``` | Technique | Fixes | Cost | Latency | |---|---|---|---| | **Contextualization** | Pronouns, ellipsis in multi-turn | 1 LLM call | ~400ms | | **Rewriting** | Vocabulary mismatch | 1 LLM call | ~400ms | | **HyDE** | Question-vs-statement asymmetry | 1 LLM call | ~800ms | | **Multi-query** | Single-phrasing brittleness | 1 call + N retrievals | ~600ms | | **Decomposition** | Multi-hop, comparison | 1 call + N retrievals + synthesis | ~2s | | **Routing** | Wrong source, wasted retrieval | 1 small call | ~200ms | ##### Query rewriting and contextualization The two are distinct and often conflated. **Rewriting** translates user vocabulary into document vocabulary. **Contextualization** resolves references to earlier turns — and it is what fixes "what about contractors". ```python from openai import OpenAI from pydantic import BaseModel client = OpenAI() class RewrittenQuery(BaseModel): standalone_query: str preserved_identifiers: list[str] reasoning: str CONTEXTUALIZE_SYSTEM = """Rewrite the user's latest message into a standalone search query, resolving all references to earlier turns. Rules: - Resolve pronouns and ellipsis ("what about X" → the full question about X). - Preserve ALL identifiers exactly: codes, clause numbers, dates, names, IDs. List them in preserved_identifiers. - Use terminology likely to appear in formal documentation. - If the message is already standalone, return it with minimal change. - Never invent details the user did not provide.""" def contextualize_query(messages, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> RewrittenQuery: """messages: the recent conversation, latest user turn last.""" history = "\n".join(f"{m['role'].upper()}: {m['content']}" for m in messages[-6:]) completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=RewrittenQuery, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": CONTEXTUALIZE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Conversation:\n{history}\n\n" f"Rewrite the latest USER message."}], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed ``` **`preserved_identifiers` is not decoration.** Rewriting is the stage most likely to silently drop a product code or clause number — the model paraphrases and `WH-4471-BLK` becomes "the black warehouse unit". Extracting identifiers explicitly lets you verify they survived, and lets you inject them into the BM25 query directly: ```python def safe_rewrite(messages, original_query): rw = contextualize_query(messages) # Verify identifiers survived; if not, append them missing = [i for i in rw.preserved_identifiers if i.lower() not in rw.standalone_query.lower()] query = rw.standalone_query if missing: query = f"{query} {' '.join(missing)}" return {"query": query, "original": original_query, "identifiers": rw.preserved_identifiers} ``` **Always retrieve for the original query as well** and fuse. Rewriting can drift, and the union is more robust than the replacement. ##### HyDE Hypothetical Document Embeddings (Gao et al., 2022) addresses a real asymmetry: **queries are questions, documents are statements**, and they live in different regions of the embedding space. The trick is to generate a *hypothetical answer* and embed that instead. A fabricated answer sits in document-space and matches real documents better than the question does — even when the fabrication is factually wrong, because the *shape* is right. ```python HYDE_SYSTEM = """Write a short passage that would answer the question, as if it were an excerpt from technical documentation. Rules: - 2-4 sentences. - Use the formal terminology such documentation would use. - Include plausible specifics (numbers, section names) — factual accuracy is NOT required; this text is used only for retrieval. - Do not hedge, do not say "I don't know", do not mention being an AI.""" def hyde_embedding(question, embedder, n_hypotheticals=1, include_original=True, model="gpt-4o-mini"): """Generate hypothetical answers, embed them, average with the query.""" import numpy as np hypotheticals = [] for _ in range(n_hypotheticals): r = client.chat.completions.create( model=model, temperature=0.7 if n_hypotheticals > 1 else 0.3, max_tokens=200, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": HYDE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": question}], ) hypotheticals.append(r.choices[0].message.content.strip()) texts = hypotheticals + ([question] if include_original else []) embeddings = embedder.encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True) pooled = embeddings.mean(axis=0) pooled = pooled / (np.linalg.norm(pooled) + 1e-9) return {"embedding": pooled, "hypotheticals": hypotheticals} ``` **Including the original query in the average is important.** Pure HyDE can drift badly on questions the model knows nothing about — it hallucinates a plausible-sounding passage about the wrong topic entirely. Averaging with the real query embedding anchors it. **Where HyDE helps and where it hurts:** | Query type | HyDE | Why | |---|---|---| | Conceptual, well-formed | **Strong gain** | Closes the question-statement gap | | Domain the model knows | **Strong gain** | Hypothetical is close to reality | | Highly specific identifiers | **Hurts** | Model fabricates around the code | | Novel or private domain | Neutral to negative | Hypothetical is unrelated | | Very short queries | Moderate gain | Gives the embedder something to work with | **Never use HyDE alone on queries containing identifiers.** Run BM25 on the original query in parallel and fuse — this is Day 21's argument applied to the transformation layer. ##### Multi-query and RAG-Fusion Generate several phrasings, retrieve for each, fuse the ranked lists. It hedges against any single phrasing being unlucky. ```python import json from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor class MultiQuerySpec(BaseModel): queries: list[str] strategy_used: list[str] MULTI_QUERY_SYSTEM = """Generate diverse search queries for the user's question. Use these strategies, one per query: 1. Formal terminology rewrite 2. A more specific sub-aspect 3. A broader framing of the topic Rules: - Preserve identifiers exactly in at least one query. - Each query must be independently searchable. - Keep each under 20 words.""" def generate_multi_queries(question, n=3, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> list[str]: completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.5, response_format=MultiQuerySpec, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": MULTI_QUERY_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Question: {question}\n" f"Generate exactly {n} queries."}], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed.queries[:n] def rag_fusion(question, retriever, n_queries=3, k=10, candidates=20, rrf_k=60, max_workers=4): """Multi-query retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion.""" queries = [question] + generate_multi_queries(question, n_queries) with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as pool: results = list(pool.map( lambda q: retriever(q, k=candidates), queries)) ranked_lists = { f"q{i}": [r["doc_id"] for r in res] for i, res in enumerate(results) } # Weight the original query higher than the generated variants weights = {f"q{i}": (1.5 if i == 0 else 1.0) for i in range(len(queries))} fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion(ranked_lists, weights=weights, k=rrf_k, top_n=k) lookup = {r["doc_id"]: r for res in results for r in res} return {"results": [{**lookup[f["doc_id"]], **f} for f in fused], "queries_used": queries} ``` **Weighting the original query at 1.5** matters. Generated variants can drift, and RRF weighted equally lets three drifted queries outvote the correct one. **Run retrievals in parallel.** Sequential multi-query is `n × retrieval_latency`; parallel is roughly one retrieval plus the generation call. **Three queries is the practical sweet spot.** Five adds latency and cost for marginal recall gain, because the variants start repeating each other. ##### Decomposition, sequenced Day 19 introduced decomposition. The subtlety worth adding here is **dependency**: some sub-queries must run in order. ```python from typing import Literal class SubQuery(BaseModel): id: str query: str depends_on: list[str] # ids of sub-queries whose answers this needs class QueryPlan(BaseModel): query_type: Literal["simple", "parallel", "sequential", "aggregation"] sub_queries: list[SubQuery] PLAN_SYSTEM = """Break the question into sub-queries and identify dependencies. query_type: - simple: answerable with one retrieval; sub_queries empty - parallel: independent sub-questions (comparisons) - sequential: later sub-queries need earlier answers (multi-hop) - aggregation: requires scanning many documents For sequential plans, use {{id}} placeholders in dependent queries, e.g. {"id": "q1", "query": "which vendor supplied the Chennai racking", "depends_on": []} {"id": "q2", "query": "notice period in the contract with {{q1}}", "depends_on": ["q1"]}""" def execute_plan(plan: QueryPlan, retriever, generator, max_sub=4): """Run sub-queries respecting dependencies.""" answers, all_chunks = {}, [] remaining = plan.sub_queries[:max_sub] for _ in range(len(remaining)): ready = [sq for sq in remaining if all(d in answers for d in sq.depends_on)] if not ready: break for sq in ready: query = sq.query for dep in sq.depends_on: query = query.replace(f"{{{{{dep}}}}}", answers[dep]) chunks = retriever(query, k=5) all_chunks.extend(chunks) answers[sq.id] = generator(query, chunks)["answer"] remaining.remove(sq) return {"sub_answers": answers, "chunks": all_chunks} ``` **The `{{q1}}` placeholder substitution is what makes multi-hop work.** Without it, "notice period in the contract with the vendor" retrieves generic contract language rather than the specific vendor's agreement. **Guard against cycles and unbounded plans.** The `for _ in range(len(remaining))` loop and `max_sub` cap are both deliberate — a plan with a circular dependency would otherwise hang. ##### Semantic routing The cheapest transformation, and often the highest-return: decide *whether and where* to retrieve before doing it. ```python from typing import Literal class RouteDecision(BaseModel): needs_retrieval: bool sources: list[Literal["handbook", "codebase", "tickets", "web"]] reasoning: str ROUTE_SYSTEM = """Decide whether the question needs document retrieval, and from which sources. needs_retrieval = false for: greetings, meta-questions about the assistant, general knowledge the model already has, follow-up clarifications. Sources: - handbook: HR policies, processes, org information - codebase: API references, code examples, architecture - tickets: past support issues and resolutions - web: current events, external product information Select the minimum set of sources that could answer the question.""" def route_query(question, conversation=None, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> RouteDecision: ctx = "" if conversation: ctx = "\n".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content'][:200]}" for m in conversation[-4:]) completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=RouteDecision, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": ROUTE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": (f"Conversation:\n{ctx}\n\n" if ctx else "") + f"Question: {question}"}], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed ``` **An embedding-based router is faster and cheaper** when your source set is stable: ```python import numpy as np class EmbeddingRouter: """Route by similarity to source descriptions. No LLM call.""" def __init__(self, embedder, source_examples: dict[str, list[str]]): self.embedder = embedder self.sources = list(source_examples) self.centroids = {} for name, examples in source_examples.items(): emb = embedder.encode(examples, normalize_embeddings=True) c = emb.mean(axis=0) self.centroids[name] = c / (np.linalg.norm(c) + 1e-9) def route(self, query, threshold=0.30, max_sources=2): q = self.embedder.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] scores = {name: float(c @ q) for name, c in self.centroids.items()} selected = [n for n, s in sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]) if s >= threshold][:max_sources] return {"sources": selected or [max(scores, key=scores.get)], "scores": {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in scores.items()}} ``` **Routing saves more than it costs.** Skipping retrieval on "thanks, that helps" eliminates a full retrieval and generation cycle. Restricting to one source instead of four cuts retrieval cost by 75%. On a mixed workload, routing typically pays for itself several times over. ##### Adaptive transformation Running every technique on every query is expensive and usually unnecessary. Gate the expensive ones on cheap signals. ```python class AdaptiveQueryPipeline: def __init__(self, retriever, embedder, router, generator, weak_score_threshold=0.42, short_query_words=6): self.retriever, self.embedder = retriever, embedder self.router, self.generator = router, generator self.weak_threshold = weak_score_threshold self.short_words = short_query_words def answer(self, question, conversation=None): trace = {"transformations": []} # 1. Cheap: contextualize only if short or has pronouns query = question if conversation and (len(question.split()) < self.short_words or _has_reference(question)): rw = safe_rewrite(conversation, question) query = rw["query"] trace["transformations"].append({"contextualize": query}) # 2. Cheap: route route = self.router.route(query) trace["transformations"].append({"route": route["sources"]}) # 3. Retrieve chunks = self.retriever(query, sources=route["sources"], k=20) # 4. Expensive: escalate ONLY if retrieval looks weak if not chunks or chunks[0]["score"] < self.weak_threshold: trace["transformations"].append({"escalate": "multi_query + hyde"}) fused = rag_fusion(query, self.retriever, n_queries=3, k=20) chunks = fused["results"] if not chunks: return {"answer": "I could not find this in the available sources.", "trace": trace} return {**self.generator(query, chunks[:5]), "trace": trace} def _has_reference(q: str) -> bool: import re return bool(re.search( r"\b(it|that|this|those|these|they|them|there|instead|also|what about)\b", q.lower())) ``` **The `_has_reference` heuristic is free** and catches most of the cases contextualization exists for. The `weak_score_threshold` escalation means expensive techniques run on the 15–20% of queries that need them rather than all of them. ##### Measuring what each technique buys ```python def compare_transformations(eval_set, retriever, embedder, k=10): """Which technique wins on which query type?""" import numpy as np import time strategies = { "baseline": lambda q, conv: retriever(q, k=k), "rewrite": lambda q, conv: retriever( safe_rewrite(conv or [{"role": "user", "content": q}], q)["query"], k=k), "hyde": lambda q, conv: retriever( embedding=hyde_embedding(q, embedder)["embedding"], k=k), "multi_query": lambda q, conv: rag_fusion(q, retriever, k=k)["results"], "decompose": lambda q, conv: _decompose_retrieve(q, retriever, k=k), } rows = [] for name, fn in strategies.items(): by_type = {} for item in eval_set: t0 = time.perf_counter() hits = fn(item["query"], item.get("conversation")) latency = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000 ids = [h["doc_id"] for h in hits] rel = set(item["relevant_ids"]) recall = len(set(ids) & rel) / max(len(rel), 1) qtype = item.get("query_type", "general") by_type.setdefault(qtype, []).append((recall, latency)) row = {"strategy": name} for qtype, vals in by_type.items(): row[f"recall_{qtype}"] = round(float(np.mean([v[0] for v in vals])), 3) row["p95_ms"] = round(float(np.percentile( [v[1] for vals in by_type.values() for v in vals], 95)), 1) rows.append(row) return rows ``` A representative result, broken down by query type: | Strategy | short | conceptual | identifier | multi-hop | p95 latency | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | baseline | 0.61 | 0.74 | **0.88** | 0.41 | 42ms | | rewrite | **0.87** | 0.79 | 0.83 | 0.46 | 448ms | | HyDE | 0.71 | **0.86** | 0.62 | 0.44 | 812ms | | multi-query | 0.79 | 0.83 | 0.85 | 0.58 | 664ms | | decompose | 0.68 | 0.77 | 0.86 | **0.89** | 2140ms | | **adaptive** | 0.85 | 0.84 | 0.87 | 0.86 | **318ms** | **No single technique wins everywhere**, and that is the finding. HyDE hurts identifier queries by 26 points. Decomposition is the only thing that touches multi-hop. Adaptive routing gets near the best of each at a fifth of the worst latency. ##### Common mistakes - **Replacing the original query** instead of fusing with it. - **Rewriting away identifiers** — extract and verify them. - **HyDE on identifier queries**, where fabrication actively hurts. - **Pure HyDE without averaging in the original embedding.** - **Sequential multi-query retrieval** instead of parallel. - **Equal RRF weights** across original and generated queries. - **Parallel execution of dependent multi-hop sub-queries.** - **Running every transformation on every query**, tripling latency for the 80% that did not need it. - **No routing**, so every query hits every source. - **Measuring aggregate recall** instead of breaking down by query type — the aggregate hides that HyDE is destroying your identifier queries. - **Unbounded decomposition** on vague questions. ##### Hands-on: break it down by query type Your practical task implements HyDE and multi-query and compares recall against direct embedding. **Segment your eval set by query type** before you start — conceptual, identifier-bearing, short, multi-hop. The aggregate number will hide the most important finding, which is that HyDE helps one segment substantially and hurts another. The mini project builds a query-transformation layer with routing and decomposition for a multi-source knowledge base. Implement the adaptive pipeline rather than a fixed chain, and log the `trace` for every query. Then examine what fraction of queries escalated to the expensive path — if it is above 40%, your `weak_score_threshold` is too high or your base retrieval needs work. The assignment evaluates HyDE, multi-query, and decomposition on complex multi-hop questions and reports which wins where. Build at least 20 genuinely multi-hop questions — ones where the answer requires chaining two lookups — and verify by hand that a single retrieval cannot answer them. Then report the per-technique breakdown with latency, and state a routing rule: which technique for which detected query type. ##### Key takeaways - **The query is the weakest link** — short, referential, and vocabulary-mismatched queries fail regardless of how good your index is. - **Rewriting must preserve identifiers explicitly.** Extract them into a list and verify they survived, because paraphrasing silently drops product codes. - **HyDE closes the question-statement asymmetry** and actively hurts identifier queries — never use it alone, and always average with the original embedding. - **Multi-hop needs sequenced sub-queries with placeholder substitution**, not parallel retrieval. - **Route first and escalate only on weak retrieval scores** — adaptive transformation reaches near-best quality on every query type at a fraction of the worst-case latency.
